analogy.p: Think of a LAN as a village. Each house has a letterbox with a unique house number (the NIC and its MAC address). The village postman (the switch) knows which house is which and delivers each letter to exactly the right house instead of pushing it through every door. The village's main post office (the router) is the place where letters for other villages are sent on towards their destination, using the full postal address (IP address). The WAP is like a messenger who lives at the village hall and carries messages by shouting across the field to people who have no letterbox cable. The analogy breaks down because real routers do not get a whole address book of the world; each router only knows the next step, and the NIC addresses are electronic, not physical.
analogy.t: The post office and the village

bullets: Describe the **purpose** of a NIC, a switch, a router and a WAP in a network.
Explain how each device is **used** when building a LAN and when connecting a LAN to the internet.
Know that the NIC is **inside** (or built into) each computer, while the switch, router and WAP are separate pieces of **network hardware**.
Know that **transmission media** (cables or radio waves) carry the signals between these devices.
Be able to **choose and justify** a set of devices for a scenario such as a school, a small office or a home.
Understand the difference between a **LAN** (one site, owned by one organisation) and a **WAN** (spread over a large area, such as the internet).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.3 (Networks, connections and protocols) asks you to understand the hardware needed to connect stand-alone computers into a **Local Area Network (LAN)**. The four items you must be able to name, describe and use in a scenario are the **network interface card (NIC)**, the **switch**, the **router** and the **wireless access point (WAP)**. Examiners rarely ask for a bare definition; they ask what a device does, why it is needed, and which devices a given organisation should buy. Learn each device as a job title: the NIC lets a device join, the switch passes data to the right device inside the network, the router links separate networks, and the WAP lets wireless devices in.

bullets: A **network** is two or more computers connected so they can share data and resources such as files, printers and an internet connection.
A **LAN** covers a small geographical area such as one building or school site and is usually owned and managed by the organisation that uses it.
A **WAN** covers a large geographical area, often joining many LANs together; the **internet** is the biggest WAN and is a network of networks.
Devices inside a LAN are normally joined by a **switch** (wired) or a **WAP** (wireless); the LAN is linked to the outside world by a **router**.
Every device that connects needs a **NIC**, because the NIC is what actually puts signals onto the cable or into the air.
Data is split into **packets** before it is sent, and the hardware handles each packet separately.
core.p: A stand-alone computer only talks to itself. To share files, printers and an internet connection, computers must be physically or wirelessly joined and must agree on how to send data to each other. Hardware does the physical work: converting data into signals, steering the signals to the right place, and linking different networks together. Without this hardware, software such as web browsers and email would have nothing to send data through.

bullets: A **wired NIC** has an **Ethernet port** (an RJ45 socket) into which a network cable is plugged; data is sent as **electrical signals** (or light if the cable is fibre).
A **wireless NIC** (WNIC) has an **antenna** and sends and receives data as **radio waves** (Wi-Fi) to and from a WAP or router.
Almost every modern laptop, phone and tablet has a wireless NIC built in, which is why they can join Wi-Fi without extra equipment.
Each NIC has a unique **MAC address** stored in it by the manufacturer, which identifies that device on the local network.
The NIC also controls **when** data is sent so that data from the computer is put on the network in an orderly way.
A desktop PC without wireless built in can have a wireless NIC added (an add-in card or a USB adapter).
Exam phrase: 'A NIC is needed so the computer can **connect to the network**' (describe: it provides the physical connection and converts data to signals).
core.p: A **NIC** (network interface card, also called a network interface controller) is the component that allows a device to connect to a network. It is a circuit that sits inside the computer, either as an add-in card or built straight onto the motherboard (in modern laptops, tablets and phones it is built in). A NIC takes the data the computer wants to send and converts it into signals that suit the transmission medium, and it receives incoming signals and converts them back into data the computer understands. Without a working NIC a device cannot join a network at all.

bullets: A MAC address is **48 bits long** and is shown as **six pairs of hexadecimal digits**.
It is **assigned by the manufacturer** and is intended to be unique to that NIC, so it identifies the hardware, not the user.
A MAC address is used **inside a LAN** to deliver data to the right device; switches use MAC addresses.
An **IP address** is used to route data **between networks**; routers use IP addresses.
Think of it as: MAC address = the permanent serial number of the NIC; IP address = a temporary postal address that depends on which network you join.
A device with two NICs (for example, Ethernet and Wi-Fi in a laptop) has **two MAC addresses**.
core.h: The MAC address on every NIC
core.p: Every NIC is given a **MAC (media access control) address** when it is made. It is a 48-bit number, normally written as 12 hexadecimal digits in six pairs, for example 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. It is used to identify one specific device on a local network, so that switches can send data to exactly the right place. It is different from an **IP address**, which identifies the device's position on a network and can change when you move to a different network.

bullets: A switch has several **ports** (commonly 8, 24 or 48); each port connects to one device or to another switch.
It receives **data packets** and forwards them to the **intended device** on the network, using the **MAC address** of the destination.
Because data goes only to the correct device, there is **less unnecessary traffic**, so the network is faster and busy devices are not slowed by data they do not need.
Sending data only to the correct device is also **more secure** than sending it to everyone, because other devices do not receive the data.
Each device on a switch can use its own connection at the same time, so many conversations can happen **simultaneously**.
Switches can be linked together to extend a network, for example one per floor of a building.
A switch works **within** one network; it does not decide how to reach other networks (that is the router's job).
core.h: The switch: connecting devices inside a LAN
core.p: A **switch** is a hardware device that connects the devices on a wired LAN together. Each computer, printer or server is connected to a port on the switch by a cable. When data arrives, the switch works out which device it is meant for and sends it **only to that device**, rather than to everyone. This is why a switch is the standard way of building a **star network**: all the devices connect to the central switch. The switch does not connect your LAN to the internet; it only joins devices inside one network.

bullets: Step 1: a data packet arrives at one port of the switch. It contains the **source MAC address** and the **destination MAC address**.
Step 2: the switch reads the **source** address and records it in its MAC table against that port, so it 'learns' where that device is.
Step 3: the switch reads the **destination** address and looks it up in the table.
Step 4: if the destination is in the table, the switch sends the packet **out of that port only**.
Step 5: if the destination is not yet known, the switch sends the packet out of **every other port** (it floods); the right device replies, and the switch then learns that address too.
Contrast (extra knowledge): a **hub** sends data to **all** ports, wasting bandwidth and letting every device see the data; a switch avoids this.
A switch does not look at IP addresses to do this job; it uses **MAC addresses** on the local network.
core.h: How a switch decides where to send data, step by step
core.p: A switch keeps a **MAC address table** that lists which MAC address is reachable through which port. It builds this table by itself by watching the data that passes through it. Understanding the steps lets you write a Higher-quality explanation and explains why a switch is better than an older device called a hub, which simply copies every packet to every port.

bullets: A router connects **two or more separate networks**, for example your LAN and your internet service provider's network.
It uses the **IP address** of the destination to decide where to send each packet.
It keeps a **routing table** with information about which direction to send packets so that they reach the destination by the **best available route**.
Because a router is attached to more than one network, it has an **address on each network** it joins.
Devices send any traffic for outside the LAN to the router's address, called the **default gateway**.
Routers also receive packets from the internet and pass them to the right device inside the LAN.
Many routers add features such as a **firewall** and give out IP addresses to the devices on the network, but the core job to state is: **connects networks and forwards packets**.
core.h: The router: joining different networks together
core.p: A **router** is a device that connects **different networks** together and forwards data packets between them. In a typical school or home, the router connects the LAN to the internet (a WAN). Data that is for another device in the same LAN stays within the LAN; data meant for the internet is sent to the router, which passes it on towards its destination. The router therefore sits at the **edge** of the network and acts as a gateway.

bullets: Step 1: the packet arrives at the router carrying the **destination IP address**.
Step 2: the router looks in its **routing table** to find the best next step towards that address.
Step 3: it sends the packet out of the correct **connection** to the next router (or to the final device if the destination is on a network it is directly attached to).
Step 4: the process is repeated at each router along the way until the packet reaches its destination network.
Because packets can take **different routes**, a busy or broken link can be avoided.
On arrival the packets are **reassembled in the correct order** to rebuild the message.
Your home router normally sends everything not on your LAN towards your internet service provider (ISP).
core.h: How a router forwards a packet, step by step
core.p: Data crossing the internet passes through many routers, each making its own decision about where the packet should go next. No single router knows the whole path; each one just chooses the best next step towards the destination. This hop-by-hop process lets the internet keep working even if some links are busy or broken, because packets can be sent by a different route.

bullets: A WAP is **wired into** the network (for example to a switch) and **transmits and receives** radio signals to and from wireless devices.
Wireless devices must have a **wireless NIC** to communicate with it.
It lets users connect **without cables**, so laptops, phones and tablets can be moved around.
It **extends** a wired network to wireless users, so wireless and wired devices can share the same files, printers and internet connection.
**Range is limited**, and walls, floors and interference reduce the signal strength, so large sites need several WAPs.
All devices on one WAP **share its bandwidth**, so too many users can slow it.
Wireless signals can be intercepted, so a WAP should use **encryption** and a strong password (a WPA2 or WPA3 key).
Exam phrase: 'A WAP allows **wireless devices** to connect to the **wired network**.'
core.p: A **wireless access point (WAP)** is a network device that allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network using **Wi-Fi** (radio waves). The WAP itself is connected to the network by a cable, usually to a switch or router, and it broadcasts a wireless signal that devices with a wireless NIC can join. In a large building you may have many WAPs placed around the site so that people can roam and still stay connected.

bullets: The **Ethernet sockets** on the box are acting as a **switch**.
The **Wi-Fi** part is acting as a **WAP**.
The part that passes data to and from the internet is acting as a **router**.
Devices inside the home use the NIC in each device to talk to the box.
A larger organisation separates the functions for **better performance, more ports, and wider coverage**.
If a question asks for one device that does all of these, 'wireless router' is a valid answer; if it asks for separate devices, name each by its job.
core.h: Home 'wireless routers' combine several devices in one box
core.p: The box your internet provider gives you is usually several devices in one case: a **router**, a small **switch** (the Ethernet sockets on the back) and a **WAP** (the Wi-Fi aerials), often with a modem as well. This is convenient and cheap for homes, but schools and businesses usually buy these as separate, more powerful devices because they need more ports, more coverage, and more control. Exam questions sometimes describe a home router, so be ready to say which function each part is performing.

bullets: 1. The laptop's **wireless NIC** turns the request into radio waves and sends them to the nearest **WAP**.
2. The WAP passes the data into the **wired network**, to a switch.
3. The **switch** reads the destination MAC address (the router's) and sends the data to the router only.
4. The **router** reads the destination IP address, sees that the web server is not on the LAN and forwards the packet towards the internet.
5. Other routers pass it on until it reaches the web server, which sends the response packets back.
6. The response returns via the router, switch and WAP, and the laptop's NIC passes the data to the browser.
Notice that the **MAC address** is used inside each network, whereas the **IP address** is used to route between networks.
core.h: Putting it together: the journey of a web request
core.p: Following a single request shows how all four devices cooperate. Imagine a student on a laptop in a school opening a web page. The request is data that must leave the laptop, cross the school's LAN and reach a web server on the internet, and then the response must travel back the same way.

bullets: **Computers in a room that need to share files and a printer**: a **switch** to link them, with a **NIC** in each.
**Staff or visitors using laptops, phones or tablets around the site**: one or more **WAPs** connected to the switch.
**Internet access or a link to another site**: a **router** connected to the ISP.
**Large building**: several switches and WAPs so every area has coverage and enough ports.
**Reliability and speed for servers or video work**: wired connections through a switch are usually faster and more stable than Wi-Fi.
**Visitor or guest access**: a WAP, usually with a separate guest network and password.
A good justification links **device + what it does + why the scenario needs it**.
core.h: Choosing devices for a scenario (how to justify)
core.p: Scenario questions reward answers that match a device to a specific need in the question. Look for clues: 'staff use laptops while moving around' suggests a WAP; 'ten computers in one room' suggests a switch; 'connected to the internet' suggests a router; every device needs a NIC. Then give a reason, not just a name.

bullets: **Switch**: connects devices in a LAN; sends data only to the intended device; uses **MAC addresses**.
**Router**: connects networks (for example LAN to internet); forwards packets by the best route; uses **IP addresses**.
**WAP**: provides **Wi-Fi** so that wireless devices can join the wired LAN; uses radio waves.
**NIC**: inside each device; provides the connection and holds the **MAC address**.
Only the **router** is needed to reach the internet; only the **WAP** is needed for wireless; the **switch** is needed for several wired devices.

If you see a question 'Explain why a switch and not a router is used to connect the computers in a room', answer that the switch links devices **within one network**, whereas a router links separate networks.
core.h: Switch, router and WAP side by side
core.p: Students most often lose marks by mixing up the three boxes. Use this contrast: the switch connects devices **inside** one wired network, the router connects **different** networks, and the WAP connects **wireless** devices to the wired network. They also use different addresses: switches use MAC addresses and routers use IP addresses.

bullets: **Topologies**: a star network has a central switch with every device connected to it; a mesh network has multiple connections between devices.
**Transmission media**: cables (copper Ethernet or fibre optic) or radio waves connect the devices to the hardware above.
**Protocols**: TCP/IP, HTTP and others describe how the data is organised; the hardware just moves the packets.
**Network security**: firewalls, encryption of Wi-Fi, passwords and MAC address filtering protect the network, and the router and WAP are common places to apply them.
**Client-server and peer-to-peer**: a switch connects the clients and the server in a client-server network.
**Internet and the cloud**: the router is the doorway from the LAN to the internet where web servers and cloud storage live.
core.p: This topic underpins several other parts of Paper 1, and examiners like answers that connect them. Knowing which device uses which type of address, and how the hardware relates to topologies, protocols and security, helps with the longer questions.

exam: **State/Give/Identify (1 mark)**: one precise fact, e.g. 'A router connects networks together'. Use the device's job, not 'it connects things'.
**Describe the purpose of a [device] (2 marks)**: two linked points, e.g. for a switch: 'connects devices in a LAN (1) and sends data only to the intended device (1)'.

Use the **exact phrases** that mark schemes reward: 'receives data packets', 'forwards to the intended device', 'connects different networks', 'allows wireless devices to connect', 'connects the device to the network'.

**Explain (3-4 marks)** needs a reason chain: point, because, so. E.g. 'A switch sends packets only to the correct device (1), using the MAC address (1), so there is less traffic and the network is faster/more secure (1).'
**Scenario questions**: pull a detail from the stem, e.g. 'staff use laptops in the corridor', and tie a device to it: 'a WAP is needed so the laptops can connect wirelessly'.

**Discuss/6-mark questions** on network design: structure your answer by device, say what it is, why this scenario needs it, and add a limitation or alternative (e.g. wired is faster, wireless is more convenient).
Always say **'wired'** for switch ports and **'wireless/Wi-Fi/radio waves'** for WAP so examiners can see you understand the difference.
Do not confuse **LAN** hardware with **WAN** hardware: a switch and a WAP are for the LAN; the router is the link to the WAN.
Name the **addresses** if asked 'how': switches use **MAC addresses**; routers use **IP addresses**.
Typical allocations: 1 mark for naming a device, 2 marks for its purpose, 4 marks for a justified recommendation, and 6 marks for a discussion with advantages, disadvantages and a conclusion.
If a question asks 'why does each computer need a NIC?', say it provides the **connection** to the network and converts data into signals that can be transmitted.

mistakes.r: A **switch** connects devices within a LAN; a **router** connects different networks, such as the LAN to the internet.
mistakes.w: A router connects the computers in the room together.

mistakes.r: A switch sends data **only to the intended device**; sending to all devices is how an old hub works.
mistakes.w: A switch sends data to every device on the network.

mistakes.r: A NIC is the **component inside the device** that lets it connect to the network; it is not the network itself.
mistakes.w: A NIC is the Wi-Fi or the internet.

mistakes.r: A WAP lets wireless devices join the **network**; the **router** is what links the network to the internet.
mistakes.w: A WAP gives you the internet.

mistakes.r: A router forwards packets between networks; a modem converts signals for the line; a WAP provides Wi-Fi. Home boxes combine them, but the functions are different.
mistakes.w: A router is the same as a modem or a WAP.

mistakes.r: The MAC address identifies the **hardware** (NIC) on the local network; the IP address identifies the device's **location** on a network and is used by routers.
mistakes.w: The MAC address is the same as the IP address.

mistakes.r: Wireless devices still need a **wireless NIC** and a **WAP** to connect to the network.
mistakes.w: Wireless means no hardware is needed.

mistakes.r: A switch reduces unnecessary traffic **inside the LAN**; internet speed depends on the connection through the router and the ISP.
mistakes.w: The switch makes the internet faster.

mistakes.r: Be specific: say **what** it connects and **how**, e.g. 'connects the LAN to the internet by forwarding packets using IP addresses'.
mistakes.w: Just say 'it connects the network' for 1 mark.

summary: OCR J277 1.3 requires you to know what a NIC, a switch, a router and a wireless access point (WAP) are, what each one does, and how they combine to build a LAN and connect it to the internet. It matters because Paper 1 asks you to describe each device and to choose and justify hardware for a given scenario.

terms.d: Network interface card: hardware inside a device that allows it to connect to a network and converts data to and from signals.
A unique 48-bit hardware address, written as six hexadecimal pairs, assigned to a NIC by the manufacturer to identify a device on a local network.
A network device that connects devices in a LAN and forwards data packets only to the intended device using its MAC address.
A device that connects different networks (such as a LAN and the internet) and forwards data packets between them using IP addresses.
A device that allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network using Wi-Fi.
Local Area Network: a network covering a small geographical area, such as a single building or site, usually managed by one organisation.
Wide Area Network: a network spanning a large geographical area, often using third-party telecommunications links. The internet is the largest.
A small unit of data that is sent across a network; it contains the data plus addressing information such as source and destination.
An address that identifies a device's location on a network and is used by routers to send packets to the correct destination.
A socket on a switch or router where a cable is plugged in, connecting one device or network.
The address of the router that a device sends data to when the destination is outside its own network.
The physical path along which data is carried, such as copper cable, fibre-optic cable or radio waves.
A standard for wired LANs in which devices are connected by cables to a switch.
Wireless technology that uses radio waves to connect devices to a network through a WAP.
A network layout where every device is connected to a central switch.
The amount of data that can be transmitted over a connection in a given time, usually in bits per second.
A list kept by a switch that records which MAC address can be reached through which port.

worked.ans: Every computer needs a NIC so that it can connect to the network (1). The 12 desktops should be connected to a switch with cables, so that data is sent only to the correct computer (1). A wireless access point is needed so that the laptops and phones in the meeting room can join the wired network using Wi-Fi (1). A router is needed to connect the office LAN to the internet by forwarding packets (1).
worked.q: A small office has 12 desktop computers in one room. Staff also use laptops and phones in a meeting room. Explain which network hardware the office needs. [4 marks]
steps: Every device needs a NIC (wired for desktops, wireless for laptops and phones).
The desktops need a switch to connect them in the LAN.
The meeting room devices need a WAP so they can connect wirelessly.
To reach the internet the office needs a router.

worked.ans: A switch connects devices within one LAN (1) and uses the MAC address to send data only to the intended device (1). A router connects different networks, such as a LAN and the internet (1) and uses the IP address to forward packets by the best route (1).
